summary: Defines an extension to SCTP that lets a host add or remove IP addresses on an existing association without tearing it down. SCTP is built to use multiple network addresses for resilience, and this lets the set of addresses change as interfaces come and go. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: SCTP was designed so that a server with several network cards could survive losing one. This RFC lets the set of addresses change while the connection is running, so a new card can be added or an old one removed without dropping the connection.

questions: can sctp add ip addresses dynamically
how does sctp add an ip address
can sctp change addresses without restarting
subtitle: How an SCTP association adds, removes and re-prefers IP addresses while it keeps running.

tldr.problem: SCTP associations can use several IP addresses for fault tolerance, but the address set was fixed at startup. Adding a network card or renumbering a network meant restarting the association, which many fault-tolerant applications treat as an outage.
tldr.mechanism: Two new chunks, ASCONF and ASCONF-ACK, carry Add IP Address, Delete IP Address and Set Primary Address requests to the peer. They are authenticated, sent one at a time, and acknowledged with correlation IDs.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can change their addresses mid-association. The price is a strict set of rules and a requirement for SCTP authentication, because address changes are a way to hijack an association.

today: RFC 5061 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 4960 and depends on the chunk authentication of RFC 4895.

sections.title: Why Addresses Need to Change
sections.content:
A local host may have several points of attachment to the Internet, which gives it some fault tolerance against hardware failures. SCTP was developed to take full advantage of such a multi-homed host, with fast failover and association survivability when a failure happens.

Many modern computers allow network cards to be added and removed while running, and a provider can renumber a network in IPv6. Either way there was a gap between full fault tolerance and what SCTP actually defined: whether a card is added or an interface is renumbered, the transport association had to be restarted to take advantage of the new configuration. For fault-tolerant applications, that restart is an outage and is undesirable.

This document describes an extension to SCTP that lets an SCTP stack add an IP address to an association, delete an IP address from it, and ask the peer to set the primary address it will use when sending to this endpoint. The dynamic addition and subtraction of addresses lets an association keep working through host and network reconfigurations.

Such a change is often brought on by the provider or by the user, and the peer might be better served by the new address, but only the endpoint where the reconfiguration happened knows that. The extension lets that endpoint advise the peer about which address it thinks the peer should use as primary.

The extension also adds a small 32-bit integer, an adaptation indication, that can be exchanged at startup. It is useful for applications that have one or more specific layers below the application but still above SCTP, because the exchange lets the right layer be enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding a network card or renumbering a network used to mean dropping the connection and starting again. This RFC lets the two ends renegotiate the address list instead.

sections.title: The ASCONF and ASCONF-ACK Chunks
sections.content:
Two new chunk types carry the control information reliably. The Address Configuration Change Chunk, ASCONF, has type 0xC1 and is used to tell the remote endpoint about a configuration change that must be acknowledged. The Address Configuration Acknowledgment Chunk, ASCONF-ACK, has type 0x80 and acknowledges the receipt.

The ASCONF chunk holds a 32-bit sequence number, whose valid range is 0 to 4294967295 and which wraps back to zero, and a mandatory address parameter of 8 or 20 bytes depending on the address type. That address is an address of the sender, and the peer must consider it part of the association. It may be used to help find the association, and if the address is 0.0.0.0 or ::0 the receiver may look the association up from other information in the packet. A host name address must not be sent and must be ignored if received. One or more request parameters follow, each in the Type-Length-Value form.

Both chunks must be sent in an authenticated way using the mechanism of RFC 4895, and a chunk received unauthenticated must be silently discarded. The ASCONF-ACK copies the sequence number from the ASCONF it acknowledges and carries one or more parameter responses.

The upper two bits of the ASCONF chunk type are set to one, so a receiver that does not understand the chunk skips it, continues processing, and reports an Unrecognized Chunk Type error. That does not abort the association, but it tells the sender not to send any further ASCONF chunks.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two new messages: one asking for a change and one answering. They must be signed, so that only the real peer can ask for an address change.

sections.title: The Seven New Parameters
sections.content:
Seven new parameters follow the format of RFC 4960. Add IP Address (0xC001) asks the peer to add an address to the association, and Delete IP Address (0xC002) asks it to remove one; both may appear only in an ASCONF chunk. Set Primary IP Address (0xC004) asks the receiver to mark an address as the one to send data to, and it may also appear in the INIT or INIT-ACK chunk to state an initial preference. Error Cause Indication (0xC003) and Success Indication (0xC005) appear only in the ASCONF-ACK.

Two more parameters can be used in the INIT or INIT-ACK: the Adaptation Layer Indication (0xC006), which carries a 32-bit adaptation code point for the upper-layer protocol and should be passed opaquely by SCTP, and the Supported Extensions parameter (0x8008).

Each request parameter carries a 32-bit correlation ID, an opaque integer that the sender chooses to identify the request. The receiver copies it into the response correlation ID of the answer, so the sender can tell which answer belongs to which request, and the receiver must not change the value.

The address parameter of an Add or Delete holds an IPv4 or IPv6 address and must not hold a broadcast or multicast address. If the address is 0.0.0.0 or ::0, an Add means that the source address of the packet is to be added, and a Delete means that all the peer's addresses except the source address are to be removed. A parameter that appears where it is not allowed may be answered with an ABORT, but a robust implementation should ignore it and leave the association intact.
sections.plainLanguage: The requests are add an address, remove an address, and use this one as the main address. Each one carries a number so that the answer can be matched to it.

sections.title: How an ASCONF Exchange Works
sections.content:
To send a change, the endpoint creates an ASCONF chunk with all the parameters it needs and a unique correlation ID for each request, and gives the chunk a sequence number. The sequence number starts at the same value as the initial transmission sequence number of the association and is incremented by one for each new chunk. If no ASCONF is outstanding, the chunk is sent; if one is, the new chunk waits until the previous one is acknowledged or times out. A T-4 retransmission timer is started, using the RTO of the selected destination address.

When the ASCONF-ACK for the last sequence number sent arrives, the timer is stopped, the error counters are cleared, and the answers are matched to the requests using the correlation IDs. If an error answer comes back for one parameter, the parameters before it count as successful if they were not reported, and the ones after it count as unsuccessful unless they carry an explicit success indication. If the peer answers with an error saying it did not recognize the ASCONF chunk type, the sender must not send any further ASCONF chunks and must stop its timer.

When the timer expires, the error counters are incremented, path and endpoint failure detection run, the RTO of the destination is doubled, and the same chunk is retransmitted, with the same sequence number and no new parameters, though an additional ASCONF may be bundled with the next sequence number. The timer is then restarted.

Several restrictions keep the transfers from causing congestion. Only one ASCONF may be in transit and unacknowledged at a time in each direction, so two may be in flight on an association, one from each endpoint. ASCONF chunks may be bundled with other chunks, in sequence number order, and the same holds for ASCONF-ACK. Neither may be sent in any state other than ESTABLISHED, SHUTDOWN-PENDING, SHUTDOWN-RECEIVED and SHUTDOWN-SENT. An ASCONF and an ASCONF-ACK should not be larger than the path MTU, and if that is unknown the minimum path MTU should be used, which is the lesser of 576 octets and the first-hop MTU for IPv4, and 1280 octets for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: One change is in flight at a time in each direction, and the sender waits for the answer before sending the next. If no answer comes, the same request is sent again, and the timer backs off.

sections.title: Rules for Adding, Deleting and Choosing a Primary
sections.content:
Adding and deleting addresses has to be done in a careful order. An address is not fully added until the ASCONF-ACK arrives, and until then the sender must not use the new address as the source of any SCTP packet except one carrying an ASCONF chunk. The receiver may use the address as a destination immediately, but must run the path verification procedure for it first, and must not send packets to it other than the ASCONF-ACK and heartbeats until the path is verified. After the ASCONF-ACK arrives, the address may be used as a source for any chunk.

When an address is being deleted, it remains a valid destination for incoming packets until the ASCONF-ACK arrives, and must not be used as a source address for any packet in the meantime. An endpoint must not delete its last remaining IP address, and must not set the source address of a packet carrying the ASCONF chunk to an address that the chunk is deleting.

Several requests are refused with a new error cause. A request to delete the last remaining address is refused with Request to Delete Last Remaining IP Address, and a request to delete the source address of the packet is refused with Request to Delete Source IP Address. A receiver without the local resources to add an address answers with Operation Refused Due to Resource Shortage, and then it must fail every later add or delete request bundled in the same ASCONF, rather than accepting a delete after rejecting an add. A sender that gets an Out of Resource error must either abort the association or not treat the address as part of it.
sections.plainLanguage: A new address only counts as added once the peer has answered, and an old address stays usable for incoming traffic until then. The last address can never be removed.

sections.title: The New Error Causes
sections.content:
Five new error causes support the new chunks and parameters. They are Request to Delete Last Remaining IP Address, Operation Refused Due to Resource Shortage, Request to Delete Source IP Address, Association Aborted Due to Illegal ASCONF-ACK, and Request Refused - No Authorization.

The last two cover the cases where the peer does something the rules do not allow. An illegal ASCONF-ACK, one that arrives for a sequence number that is greater than or equal to the next one to be used while no ASCONF is outstanding, aborts the association. And a request that the peer is not authorized to make is refused with the no-authorization cause.
sections.plainLanguage: Five new reasons for saying no, covering everything from trying to remove the last address to trying to change an address the peer has no authority to change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Adding or deleting an IP address on an existing association gives an extra way to hijack an association, so the RFC requires the authentication mechanism of RFC 4895 to limit what an attacker can do. Hijacking an association this way is only possible for an attacker who can intercept the first two packets of the association setup when the SCTP-AUTH extension is used without pre-shared keys, and the extension must then be used with a preconfigured shared key.

When the address parameter of an Add, Delete or Set Primary request is a wildcard, the source address of the packet is used, and that address is not protected by SCTP-AUTH, so an on-path attacker can rewrite it. A wildcard Add lets the attacker add an address of its choosing, which does little immediate damage but can set up later attacks. A wildcard Delete lets the attacker cause every address but one to be deleted, and the surviving address might be one the attacker controls. A wildcard Set Primary lets the attacker make an address the primary one. Using a wildcard Add and a wildcard Set Primary together gives the attacker more to work with. Endpoints that believe they face this threat should not use wildcard addresses.

Two more rules follow from the same concern. An endpoint that supports this extension and receives an INIT saying the peer supports ASCONF but not RFC 4895 must send an ABORT, or may silently discard the INIT, but must never proceed by sending an INIT-ACK. And an endpoint that receives such an INIT-ACK must not send the COOKIE-ECHO; it must discard the INIT-ACK and report that the association cannot be established.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the addresses of a live connection is a way to steal it, so the change messages must be signed, and a peer that cannot sign them must not be allowed to set the connection up.

items.desc: Carries the error causes in an ASCONF-ACK.

items.desc: Asks the peer to prefer an address when sending.

items.desc: Reports success for a request parameter.

items.title: Delete last address
items.text: The peer may not remove the last remaining address of an association.

items.title: Resource shortage
items.text: The peer has no resources to add the address.

items.title: Delete source address
items.text: The peer may not delete the address the request came from.

items.title: Illegal ASCONF-ACK
items.text: An acknowledgment for a sequence number that was never sent, which aborts the association.

items.title: No authorization
items.text: The peer is not allowed to make the requested change.
